how.title: How it was calculated
how.fireball.body: The fireball is the ball of glowing air and weapon debris. Everything inside it is vaporised. Its size is taken at the moment the blast wave breaks away from it, and doubled, as the source suggests for the largest size.
how.fireball.uncertainty: The source itself calls the largest size 'not well defined'.
how.blast.body: The blast wave raises the air pressure for a moment. The peak overpressure at each distance comes from measured height-of-burst curves for a 1 kiloton burst, and is scaled to other yields with the cube root of the yield: eight times the yield doubles every distance.
how.blast.uncertainty: Stated accuracy of the fit to the curves. Hills, buildings and weather change the real pressure.
how.thermal.body: About a third of the energy leaves the fireball as heat and light. The energy that reaches a surface falls with the square of the distance, and the air absorbs part of it on the way. Burns depend on the energy received and on how fast it arrives, which is why the threshold rises with yield.
how.thermal.uncertainty: The source gives 25 % for the emitted energy. Haze, cloud and anything in the line of sight change the result much more.
how.radiation.body: In the first minute the burst sends out neutrons and gamma rays. The dose is the sum of three parts read from the charts of the source. For fission weapons the source prints a lower and an upper curve, because weapons differ; the ring is shown as the span between them.
how.radiation.uncertainty: The source gives a factor of 0.5 to 2 for these charts. Walls and soil reduce the dose strongly.
how.fallout.body: When the fireball touches the ground, soil is drawn into the cloud and falls back, radioactive, along the wind. The pattern comes from WSEG-10, a standard model of the 1960s to 1980s: stretched along the effective wind, widened by wind shear. Dose rates are given for one hour after the burst and fall quickly: seven times later, ten times weaker.
how.fallout.uncertainty: Fallout models agree with each other only within a factor of about two, and real patterns are irregular.
how.casualties.body: The number of people living at each distance is multiplied by the share that is killed or injured there. The result is a range: the low end takes the assumptions that give fewer casualties, the high end those that give more.
how.casualties.blast: Blast: share of people by overpressure zone
how.casualties.range: What differs between the low and the high end
how.casualties.exposed: People in direct sight of the fireball
how.casualties.transmission: Initial radiation that gets through walls
how.casualties.burns: Burns: people in direct sight of the fireball inside the third-degree ring are counted as killed, inside the second-degree ring as injured.
how.casualties.radiation: Initial radiation: 300 rem kills about 10 %, 450 rem half and 600 rem 90 % of those exposed.
how.casualties.uncertainty: The source calls its own table 'relatively conservative' and stresses that nobody can calculate such numbers with precision. The population grid counts residents, so a city centre by day holds more people than the estimate assumes.

settings.about.text: Atomic Atlas shows what nuclear explosions do: blast, heat, radiation and fallout, on a real map. It is built for learning, with public scientific models and the source of every number one click away.
settings.about.limits: It simulates effects only. It does not choose targets and holds nothing about how weapons are made.
settings.about.mapData: Maps: OpenFreeMap, © OpenMapTiles, data from OpenStreetMap contributors. Built-in map: Natural Earth. Satellite images: Sentinel-2 cloudless by EOX. Terrain: Mapzen / AWS Terrain Tiles.
catalog.title: Weapons catalog
catalog.intro: Published figures from open sources. Choosing a yield puts it into the scenario.
catalog.estimate.hint: This country does not publish these figures. They are estimates by outside analysts.
globe.hint: Click the globe to place the launch point, then the targets
missiles.title: Missile flight
missiles.choose.hint: Pick a missile from the catalog to see how far it reaches and how it flies.
missiles.shape.minimumEnergy.hint: The path that reaches the target with the least speed.
missiles.shape.lofted.hint: Steeper: higher and slower to arrive. Needs more speed.
missiles.shape.depressed.hint: Flatter: lower and quicker. Needs more speed.
missiles.shape.reach: With the same speed, on this path it reaches {range}.
missiles.glide.hint: A rocket lifts the glider into the upper air and lets it go, fast and level. From there it flies on its own lift, between about 55 and 25 km up, slowed by the air all the way, and at the end it dives on its target. It flies far lower than a ballistic missile, but over intercontinental distances it is not faster: the air takes away its speed.
missiles.glide.reach: From its published speed, the glide model takes it {range} before it slows below Mach 5.
missiles.cruise.high: Supersonic: it is timed at its published speed high up, in the stratosphere, where the sources give its speed and range.
missiles.cruise.published: It is timed at its published speed, close to the ground.
missiles.cruise.typical: No speed is published for this missile: it is timed at a typical subsonic speed, {speed}.
missiles.place.launch.hint: The next click on the globe sets where the missile is launched from. The dashed ring shows its range.
missiles.place.target.hint: Each click on the globe adds a target, one per warhead.
missiles.warning.needsSea: This missile is launched from a submarine or ship: place the launch point at sea.
missiles.warning.needsLand: This missile is launched from land: place the launch point on land.
missiles.outOfRange: Out of range: this missile reaches {range}.
missiles.arrived.many: All warheads have come down. Choose a flight above to see the effects there.
missiles.assumptions: Times are for the coasting part of the flight on a round Earth that does not turn. The powered climb adds a few minutes. Cruise missiles are timed at their published speed, or at a typical subsonic speed when none is published. Every warhead can be given any target within range; on a real missile the warheads of one launch come down much closer together. Hypersonic gliders are timed from the start of their glide, taken over the launch point.
quantity.flightPathAngle: Climb angle when the engines stop
quantity.glideSpeed: Speed at the start of the glide
quantity.diveSpeed: Speed when it dives on the target
quantity.soundSpeed: Speed of sound where it flies
how.trajectory.title: Ballistic flight
how.trajectory.body: Once its engines stop, a ballistic missile coasts like a thrown stone: on an ellipse around the centre of the Earth that happens to meet the ground. The distance fixes the ellipse, and the ellipse gives the speed needed, the highest point and the time.
how.trajectory.uncertainty: The powered climb, the turning of the Earth and the air on the way down are left out. Real flight times are a few minutes longer.
how.cruise.title: Cruise flight
how.cruise.body: A cruise missile flies through the air like an aircraft, at a steady speed. The time is the distance divided by its published speed, or by a typical subsonic speed when none is published. A speed given as a Mach number is turned into km/h with the speed of sound where the missile flies: near the ground for a subsonic missile, in the stratosphere for a supersonic one, where the sources give its speed and range.
how.cruise.uncertainty: Real routes are not straight, and the speed changes along the way: the climb after launch and any low flying near the end are not modelled.
how.glide.title: Hypersonic glide
how.glide.body: A glider flies on its own lift in the upper air. At each speed it settles at the height where its lift, together with the outward pull of flying round the Earth, carries its weight; as the air slows it down, it sinks lower. With lift and drag in a fixed ratio, how fast it slows depends on its speed alone, which gives its range and its time in closed form.
how.glide.uncertainty: The figures of a published test glider (the HTV-2) are used, as no other glider’s are public. The boost, the pull-up into the glide and the dive are not modelled, and the path is straight, without turns.
playback.title: Watch it happen
playback.hint: Plays the detonation on the map, timed by the same models: the fireball, the heat, the blast wave reaching each ring, the cloud.
playback.drift: Carried by the wind {distance} to the {direction}, at {speed}. Fallout comes down along its way.
playback.drift.calm: No wind: the cloud stays over ground zero.
playback.fallout.rest: In the hours after, the rest of the fallout comes down along the wind, out to {distance} from ground zero, where its weakest contour (1 R/h at one hour) closes.
playback.fallout.none: Burst too high for local fallout: the cloud keeps its radioactivity high up, and it comes down thinly, days later and far away.
playback.event.heatPeak: The fireball is at its brightest
playback.event.heatMost: Most of the heat has been given off
playback.event.blast20: Blast wave reaches the 20 psi ring
playback.event.blast5: Blast wave reaches the 5 psi ring
playback.event.blast2: Blast wave reaches the 2 psi ring
playback.event.blast1: Blast wave reaches the 1 psi ring
playback.event.cloudStable: The mushroom cloud has its full size (about 10 minutes)
how.arrival.title: Timing of the explosion
how.arrival.body: The blast wave is a shock front. The stronger it is, the faster it moves, well above the speed of sound close in and at the speed of sound far out. Following the front outwards at the speed that belongs to its strength gives the time at which it reaches each distance. The heat arrives at once and lasts a few seconds. The fireball rises and becomes the head of the mushroom cloud: its top climbs for a few minutes and the head keeps spreading until about 10 minutes, to the height and width the source gives for the yield; the stem is dust drawn up from the ground.
how.arrival.uncertainty: Within about 15 % of the arrival-time charts of the source. The growth of the fireball and the rise of the cloud are rough averages; fires and their spread are not simulated.
infra.title: Infrastructure in the affected area
infra.hint: General findings for the kind of installation, not an assessment of the place itself.
infra.more: and {count} more inside the blast rings
infra.airport.none: Aircraft parked in the open: no damage expected.
infra.airport.light: Aircraft parked in the open: light damage, they can still fly.
infra.airport.moderate: Aircraft parked in the open: moderate damage, repairs on the airfield before they can fly.
infra.airport.severe: Aircraft parked in the open: severe damage, major repairs before they can fly.
infra.power.none: Electricity network: weaker than in the tests of the source; little damage expected.
infra.power.light: Electricity network: less than in the 5 psi test, where the damage was like that of a severe storm.
infra.power.moderate: Electricity network: as in the test at 5 psi. Poles and a pylon down, substation still usable by hand; repairs in about a day.
infra.power.beyond: Electricity network: stronger than the tests of the source (5 psi). Heavier damage is to be expected; the source gives no figures.
how.infrastructure.body: The map shows airports and power stations from open datasets. For those inside the blast rings, the peak overpressure at their distance is compared with what the source reports for that kind of installation: the damage table for parked aircraft, and the two tests of a complete electricity system at 5 and at 1.7 psi.
how.infrastructure.uncertainty: The findings come from tests with yields of some tens of kilotons. For megaton yields the blast lasts longer and damage at the same overpressure may be greater. Buildings of the installations themselves follow the blast rings.
how.infrastructure.data: Airports: OurAirports (public domain). Power stations: Global Power Plant Database 1.3, World Resources Institute (CC BY 4.0), stations of 100 MW and more.
settings.offline.hint: Areas without internet: download the detailed map of the area now on screen, down to street level. There the map then works offline.
settings.offline.population: With each area the app also downloads its population at 100 m, for closer casualty estimates there: a temporary download of 20–170 MB from the European Commission's JRC, of which a few MB are kept.
settings.offline.download: Download the area on screen ({tiles} tiles)
settings.offline.tooLarge: The area on screen is too large to download. Zoom in to a city or a region first.
settings.offline.error: The download did not finish. Check the internet connection and try again.
settings.offline.missing: {tiles} map tiles could not be downloaded whole; the map has gaps there without internet. Download the area again to fill them in.
closeup.title: From close up
closeup.failed: The 3D picture cannot be shown on this device. The numbers and findings below are the same.
closeup.hint: A general scene, not the real place: it shows what these effects do to ordinary buildings, vehicles and installations. The spread of fires is not simulated.
closeup.building.light: Buildings: light damage. Windows and doors broken, roofs and light walls damaged.
closeup.building.severe: Buildings: badly damaged. Houses need major repairs before they can be lived in.
closeup.building.collapse: Buildings: most houses collapse. Stronger buildings are badly damaged.
closeup.building.destroyed: Buildings: destroyed, also heavy concrete ones.
closeup.vehicles.overturned: Vehicles: overturned and thrown where they stand side-on to the blast.
closeup.vehicles.standing: Vehicles: stay on their wheels; glass and bodywork may be damaged.
closeup.fires.start: Fires: paper, curtains and dry leaves catch fire (from about {exposure} for this yield).
closeup.fires.none: Fires: the heat here is below what sets paper alight (about {exposure} for this yield).
closeup.ship.severe: Ships: sunk, capsized or damaged beyond repair (merchant ships, Glasstone & Dolan Fig. 5.146).
closeup.ship.moderate: Ships: immobilised; engines, boilers and equipment need extensive repairs.
closeup.ship.none: Ships: no serious damage from the blast; equipment may be damaged.
closeup.waves: Waves here: about {height} crest to trough.
closeup.reactor.notModelled: Reactor building (outlined): not modelled. No public general model gives blast damage to it, so none is shown. What a release of radioactivity does can be explored in Accidents.
closeup.dam.notModelled: Dam (outlined): not modelled. Whether a dam fails depends on how it is built, which no public model describes. On the map, “What if it fails?” shows where the water would go.
accident.map.hint: Click the map to place the release · right-click a point for the dose there
accident.title: Release into the air
accident.note.chernobyl-1986: Released over about ten days in changing winds and carried high by the fire; one steady plume is a coarse picture of it.
accident.note.fukushima-2011: Released over weeks from three reactors; much of it blew out over the Pacific.
accident.note.kyshtym-1957: The 74 PBq that the plume carried beyond the site; nine tenths of the 740 PBq came down within 5 km.
accident.note.windscale-1957: A fire in a graphite reactor that burned for three days. The polonium-210 it also released is not in this model.
accident.note.three-mile-island-1979: Almost only noble gases; the containment held nearly everything else.
accident.place.historical: Use the place of this accident
accident.place.hint: Or click anywhere on the map. The amount stays the one chosen above. With the historical place come the duration and height its source reports.
accident.stability.A: A: very unstable. Strong sun, light wind: the plume mixes quickly upwards and sideways.
accident.stability.B: B: unstable. Sunny day with a moderate wind.
accident.stability.C: C: slightly unstable. Bright day with wind.
accident.stability.D: D: neutral. Overcast or windy, day or night: the usual choice.
accident.stability.E: E: slightly stable. Night with some cloud and light wind.
accident.stability.F: F: stable. Clear, calm night: the plume stays narrow and close to the ground for a long way.
accident.run.hint: Place the release on the map first.
accident.criteria: Where protective action would be warranted
accident.iodine: Iodine thyroid blocking ({dose} to the thyroid in 7 days)
accident.urgent: Sheltering or evacuation ({dose} in the first 7 days)
accident.relocation: Temporary relocation ({dose} in the first year)
accident.criteria.hint: Distances along the middle of the plume, for a person out of doors the whole time. Generic criteria of the International Atomic Energy Agency.
accident.iodine.hint: The thyroid dose is that of an adult breathing in radioiodine while the plume passes. Per becquerel breathed in, a one-year-old's dose is about ten times an adult's (ICRP 119), though a small child breathes in less air.
accident.table: Dose along the middle of the plume
accident.table.hint: Dose from breathing while the plume passes, from the cloud and from what settles on the ground. The thyroid column is the dose to an adult's thyroid from the radioiodine breathed in; the last column is the caesium-137 left on the ground.
accident.assumptions: One steady wind over flat, open country; no rain, hills or buildings. Nothing is washed away or decays other than by its half-life, and nobody takes shelter: the ground dose is an upper estimate, more so over a year. Food and water are not counted. Beyond about 100 km a single steady wind is no longer a fair picture.
accident.legend: Outlines: dose in the first year
accident.legend.iodine: Dashed: iodine thyroid blocking ({dose} to the thyroid in 7 days)
how.plume.title: Dose from a release
how.plume.body: The released material is carried by the wind and spreads sideways and upwards as it goes, faster in unstable air. This gives the amount of each radionuclide that passes a place. A person there breathes some of it in, is irradiated by the passing cloud, and afterwards by what has settled on the ground. Each of the three is the amount times a dose coefficient for that radionuclide. The dose to the thyroid counts only the radioiodine breathed in: its effective dose coefficient divided by the weight of the thyroid in the effective dose, 0.05, because nearly all of the dose from iodine is to the thyroid.
how.plume.uncertainty: A plume model of this kind is usually right within a factor of a few for a short release in steady weather over open country, and can be far off for long releases in changing weather, in rain or among hills. The ground dose assumes a person out of doors all the time with no weathering.
quantity.dose7dAt10km: Dose in the first 7 days at 10 km
quantity.dose1yAt10km: Dose in the first year at 10 km
quantity.thyroidAt10km: Dose to an adult's thyroid at 10 km
water.title: Water waves
water.depth.coarse: from coarse sea-floor data: change it if you know it
water.depth.needed: Ground zero is on water, but the map holds no depth here. Enter the depth of the water to see the waves.
water.reading: Reading the depth of the water at ground zero…
water.airburst: Ground zero is over water, but this is an air burst: it puts little of its energy into the water. The wave relations used here are for a burst at the surface or under it.
water.flood.unavailable: The height of the land around could not be read, so the flooded area is not shown.
water.flood.none: No land within {radius} is low enough for the waves to flood.
water.hint: Wave heights are crest to trough, over water as deep as at ground zero. Waves from an explosion are short: they break near the burst and again on the shore, so far away they are modest. The flooded area is an upper estimate.
dams.title: Dams nearby
dams.flood.loading: Following the water down the valley…
dams.flood.third: Peak falls to a third after
dams.flood.tenth: Peak falls to a tenth after
dams.flood.end.water: The water reaches a lake or the sea.
dams.flood.end.flat: The way ends where the land becomes flat; the water spreads out from there.
dams.flood.end.length: Shown for the first 50 km; by then the peak has fallen below 1 %.
dams.flood.unavailable: The height of the land could not be read, so the way of the water is not shown.
dams.hint: Whether a dam would fail depends on how it is built, which no public model of nuclear effects describes. “What if it fails?” shows what would follow if it did, from general relations for dam failures.
how.water.title: Water waves
how.water.height.title: Height of the waves
how.water.height.body: An explosion in or on the water throws up a ring of waves. Their height falls about as one over the distance. In shallow water less of the energy goes into the waves, so the height also depends on the depth.
how.water.height.uncertainty: The heights are capped where a wave cannot stand: by the depth in shallow water and by the steepest a wave can be in deep water.
how.water.speed.title: When the waves arrive
how.water.speed.body: No wave on the water runs faster than the square root of gravity times the depth, and the first waves travel close to that. The highest wave of the train, with the period given by Glasstone & Dolan, travels at its group speed.
how.water.shore.title: At the shore
how.water.shore.body: As a wave runs into shallower water it grows (Green’s law) until it breaks, at a height of about 0.78 times the depth. The height of the breaking wave is taken as how high the water runs up the land, and all land lower than that, connected to the sea, is shown as flooded.
how.water.shore.uncertainty: Real waves lose height as they run inland, so the area shown is too large on flat land.
how.dam.title: If a dam fails
how.dam.outflow.title: Peak flow out of the breach
how.dam.outflow.body: An empirical relation fitted to dam failures gives the highest flow out of the breach from the volume of water behind the dam and its depth. The height of the dam stands in for the depth: a full reservoir.
how.dam.outflow.uncertainty: The relation was fitted to earthfill dams; for concrete dams, which can fail more suddenly, it is an order of magnitude only.
how.dam.attenuation.title: Down the valley
how.dam.attenuation.body: The flood wave spreads out as it runs down the valley and its peak falls. The way of the water is found by walking downhill on the terrain from the dam; the peak flow is shown falling to 37 % over every 10 km.
how.dam.attenuation.uncertainty: Wide floodplains take more of the water, narrow valleys less.
quantity.damHead: Depth of the water at the dam
war.title: War scenario
war.add: Add this launch to the scenario
war.add.hint: Set up a launch above, choose when it happens, and add it. Add as many as you like, from different places and weapons: they play on one clock.
war.defence.hint: In general terms only: in which part of a flight a defence could act, and the share of warheads that would get through if each layer fired a number of shots, each with the chance of success you set. Real systems and their performance are not described.
war.boost.hint: 170 s (solid) to 240 s (liquid) for the model ICBMs of the APS study
war.event.terminal: Launch {salvo}, warhead {target}: below the terminal height
war.casualties.unavailable: The population data could not be read.
war.casualties.hint: Each warhead as an air burst at the height that maximises damage to houses; each target's estimate counts as much as the chance its warhead gets through. Targets close together count the same people twice. Fallout, fires and what follows are not included.
war.winter.hint: The smoke of burning cities can cool the whole planet and cut harvests for years. The app does not calculate this; it shows the cases of a published study. The soot depends on what burns, which the app does not model.
war.winter.closest: The yield expected to arrive in this scenario ({yield}) is closest to the case with {soot} Tg of soot.
war.winter.below: The yield expected to arrive in this scenario ({yield}) is much smaller than in any case of the study; the smallest ({soot} Tg of soot) already cut food production worldwide.
war.winter.above: The yield expected to arrive in this scenario ({yield}) is larger than in any case of the study; the largest gave {soot} Tg of soot.
war.winter.cooling: In the study the average temperature over the world's crop regions fell by up to {low} °C (5 Tg) to {high} °C (150 Tg), most within 1–2 years, and stayed lower for more than 10 years.
war.assumptions: Every launch, target and time is placed by you; the app does not choose or rank targets.
how.defence.title: Missile defence
how.defence.body: If every shot is independent and destroys its target with chance p, a warhead survives one shot with chance 1 − p and n shots with chance (1 − p)^n. A warhead that has to pass several layers survives all of them with the product of those chances. A layer counts only for flights that have that phase: a flight that stays low has no midcourse, a cruise missile only a terminal phase.
how.winter.body: Xia and colleagues ran a climate model, crop models and a fishery model for six war scenarios, from 100 weapons of 15 kt on cities (5 Tg of soot in the stratosphere) to 4,400 weapons of 100 kt (150 Tg). The table gives their numbers. The case shown as closest is the one whose number of weapons times their yield is nearest, on a logarithmic scale, to the yield expected to arrive in this scenario.
how.winter.uncertainty: The soot depends above all on how much city burns, which differs from target to target. The study's numbers of people without food assume no trade between countries and are for the population of 2010.

settings.voice.browser: The browser's own voice speaks, in the language of the app. Nothing to download.
settings.voice.browser.missing: This browser has no voice for this language. A browser on another system, or the app, may have one.
settings.voice.browser.onlyMale: This browser has only a male Greek voice. Greek is spoken by a female voice only, so the voice stays off here.
settings.voice.download.hint: After each simulation the app can say a short summary out loud, and the assistant's answers. The voice works offline; it is downloaded once (about 150 MB: the Piper speech engine with one Greek and one English voice). The app never listens.
settings.voice.error: The download did not finish. Check the internet connection and try again.
settings.voice.on: Speak after each simulation and assistant answer
settings.voice.on.hint: A short summary of the result, and the assistant's answers, in the language of the app

assistant.title: Assistant
assistant.askAbout: Explain the result “{topic}” on screen: what it means and how it was calculated.
assistant.unsupported: The assistant is not available on this system yet.
assistant.download.hint: The assistant explains results and sets up simulations when you ask in words. It runs on this device only, without internet once downloaded. Choose a size:
assistant.download.sizes: The small one runs on most computers; the large one answers better and needs about 8 GB of memory. A graphics card makes both much faster.
assistant.download.sizes.phone: The small one suits most phones; the large one answers better and needs a phone with 8 GB of memory. Answers take longer than on a computer, and the phone warms up while it works.
assistant.download.runtime: Windows will also install the Microsoft Visual C++ runtime, which the assistant needs, and will ask for your permission once.
assistant.download.error: The download did not finish. Check the internet connection and try again.
assistant.welcome: Ask about the results, or ask for a simulation in words, for example “A 300 kt burst at the surface” or “Compare 15 kt and 1 Mt”. Place ground zero on the map first.
assistant.error: The assistant did not answer. Try again in a moment.
assistant.refuse: That is outside what Atomic Atlas does. It shows the effects of nuclear explosions from public models; it does not help to make or get weapons, choose targets or get past defences. Ask me about the results, or for a simulation.
assistant.limits: The assistant only uses the app's own calculations and catalog. It does not choose targets and gives nothing about how weapons are made. Small local models can be wrong: the numbers on screen and their sources are what count.
assistant.tool.set_detonation: Setting the yield and the burst…
assistant.tool.explain_effect: Reading the explanation and its source…
downloads.title: Downloads
downloads.intro: Atomic Atlas also comes as an app, with an offline assistant, a downloadable voice, the population at 100 m and map areas kept offline. Free, from GitHub; each link gives the newest version.
downloads.qr.hint: Scan this code with the phone to download the app.
downloads.apk.hint: Android asks to allow installing apps from this source: allow it, for this one install.
downloads.deb.hint: Double-click the file, or run: sudo apt install ./atomic-atlas-linux-amd64.deb
downloads.exe.hint: The installer is not digitally signed, so Windows shows a blue warning: choose "More info", then "Run anyway".
downloads.ios: There is no app for iPhone or iPad: this web version is the way to use Atomic Atlas there.
